title: How many gods? One
hookLine: the last challenger asks how many gods there are, and keeps asking until the number counts down to one
carry: truth is one; the wise call it many names

cards: People sometimes say Hindus have three hundred thirty million gods. The Upanishad has its own count, and it's a countdown. The last challenger, Vidagdha Shakalya, asks Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there?
Three thousand three hundred and six, he answers. Yes, says Shakalya. But how many gods are there, really?
Thirty-three. Yes, but how many really? Six.

teach.b: Then Shakalya makes him explain each number. The three thousand and more, Yajnavalkya says, are only their powers.

There are really thirty-three: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Adityas, and Indra and Prajapati. The Vasus are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, sun, sky, moon and stars: everything dwells in them.

The Rudras are the ten breaths in a person, and the self: when they leave the body, they make people weep. The Adityas are the twelve months, carrying everything along. Indra is the thunder; Prajapati is the sacrifice.
The six are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, the sun and the sky. The three are the three worlds.

teach.h: FOOD AND BREATH; THE WIND; THEN BREATH.
teach.b: The two are food and breath. The one and a half? The wind that blows, because everything grows in it.
It's a pun in Sanskrit; it doesn't translate. And the one? Breath.
It is Brahman. They call it That. Notice what didn't happen: the countdown never says the many gods were a mistake.
They fold onto one, like a fan folding shut.
A verse in the Rig Veda says it in a single line: ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti.

teach.h: TRUTH IS ONE; THE WISE CALL IT MANY NAMES.
teach.b: Truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. Hindus live this in different ways. Some worship one form of God as supreme, and see the others as that God's forms or helpers.
Others honor many deities, each in its place. Advaita teachers hear in the count one reality appearing as many. This passage gives all of them room.
So when a friend asks how many gods Hindus have, the honest answer is both: many forms, one truth.

how: Hindu traditions hold many forms of the divine together with the conviction that the divine is one; ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti from the Rig Veda is often quoted for that idea, and the thirty-three gods are named in Vedic ritual.

o: the king who sets the prize of a thousand cows
the sage who answers every question in the court
the last challenger, who counts the gods down to one

p: the ten breaths and the self

s: the text says the thirty-three gods were a mistake
it keeps them, and shows them folding down to one.
"330 million gods" is a count this passage gives
it counts 3,306, then 33, then down to one.
the twelve Adityas are explained as the twelve months

games.q: Shakalya asks: how many gods are there, really? you're Yajnavalkya, and you've already said 3,306. what's your next answer?
games.why: thirty-three, and then six, three, two, one and a half, and one. each step folds the last one in, and keeps it.

practice: Start wide: notice everything you can hear and feel at once, the many. Then narrow to three things, then two, the air coming in and the body receiving it, then one and a half, the breath moving, then one: just breath.
When the many come back, and they will, count down again, gently.

wordCard.voice: Vidagdha Shakalya. The challenger whose questions counted the gods down to ekam, one: breath, Brahman, That.

orig.note: Sanskrit ekam: one. ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti, truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways (Rig Veda 1.164.46).

carryVoice: Your line: truth is one; the wise call it many names. Tomorrow, Shakalya keeps on asking, and it costs him dearly. Rest well.
